I will keep the same wheat-maize rotation on all 8.0 mu, because that is what fits my land, my water, and my labor. I do not start from zero. I start from last year's practice and then adjust a little. I have well irrigation, so I will push yield a bit instead of farming too cautiously. On 8 mu, I can still manage carefully, but I also need the work to stay simple because only two people are in the household and some labor goes off-farm.

For winter wheat, I will use an improved variety, not an old local one. Around here, if wheat stands well through winter and I do not let fertilizer run short at jointing, yield is more stable. I will put most of the phosphorus and potassium in as base fertilizer and split the nitrogen, because wheat needs steady feeding, not all at once. Since I have water from the well, I will plan for three irrigations in a normal year. If spring is very dry, I will not hesitate to add water on time, because losing wheat heads is more costly than spending a bit more on pumping.

For summer maize, I will use hybrid seed. I have farmed long enough to know maize responds clearly to seed quality and nitrogen, especially after wheat. I will not cut fertilizer too hard, because maize can lose yield fast if it turns pale early or suffers around tasseling. I will keep phosphorus and potassium moderate but not omit them, because continuous wheat-maize rotation pulls nutrients out every year. I will keep maize management simple: fast sowing after wheat harvest, fewer field passes, and timely water if rain does not come. That saves labor and protects yield.
